content: Chlorosis, also referred to as green sickness, is a specific type of anemia characterized by a greenish tint to the skin of affected individuals. The clinical manifestations of this condition include fatigue, shortness of breath, dyspepsia, headaches, erratic or diminished appetite, and amenorrhea. In modern medical terminology, this condition is now recognized as hypochromic anemia. In 1554, the German physician Johannes Lange described chlorosis as a condition predominantly affecting virgins. He suggested that the cure involved engaging in sexual activity and conceiving, as he believed this would restore health. The term chlorosis was later introduced in 1615 by Jean Varandé, a professor of medicine in Montpellier, deriving the name from the Greek word Chloris, which translates to greenish-yellow, pale green, pale, or fresh. Both Lange and Varandé cited Hippocrates as a reference for their understanding of the condition. Historically, chlorosis was also referred to as morbus virgineus (virgin's disease) or febris amatoria (lover's fever). In 1811, Francis Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue defined green sickness as a disease of unmarried women caused by celibacy. In 1681, the English physician Thomas Sydenham classified chlorosis as a hysterical disorder, which he believed affected not only adolescent girls but also slender and frail women who appeared consumptive. Sydenham advocated for the use of iron as a treatment, stating that it revitalized the worn-out or languid blood, thereby invigorating the animal spirits that had been weakened and suppressed. In 1872, the French physician Armand Trousseau also recommended iron therapy for chlorosis, though he similarly categorized it as a nervous disease. By 1887, Andrew Clark, a physician at London Hospital, proposed a physiological explanation for chlorosis, linking its onset to the physical demands of growth and menarche in adolescent girls. In 1895, Ralph Stockman, a pathologist at the University of Edinburgh, conducted experiments demonstrating that inorganic iron played a critical role in hemoglobin synthesis. He concluded that chlorosis could be attributed to iron deficiency, which was exacerbated by menstrual blood loss and inadequate dietary intake. Despite Stockman's findings and the proven efficacy of iron supplementation in alleviating the symptoms of chlorosis, debates regarding its etiology persisted into the 1930s. In 1937, Arthur J. Patek and Clark W. Heath of Harvard Medical School definitively concluded that chlorosis was identical to hypochromic anemia.
